canonical_statement: Multiple myeloma accounts for about 1% of all cancers and approximately 10% of hematologic malignancies.
The review reports more than 36,000 new U.S. multiple myeloma cases and almost 11,000 deaths per year.
The median age at diagnosis of multiple myeloma is about 65 years.

population.label: Patients with multiple myeloma at diagnosis

canonical_statement: Extramedullary disease is present in approximately 1%–2% of patients at initial diagnosis and develops later in about 8%.
MGUS is present in approximately 5% of the population older than 50 years and progresses to myeloma or a related malignancy at about 1% per year.
Smoldering multiple myeloma progresses at approximately 10% per year for the first 5 years, 3% per year for the next 5 years, and 1.5% per year thereafter.
t(4;14), del(17p), and gain(1q) are associated with higher progression risk from MGUS or smoldering multiple myeloma.
Multiple myeloma diagnosis requires at least 10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma plus at least one myeloma-defining event.
Hypercalcemia qualifies as a myeloma-defining CRAB feature when serum calcium is >1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL.
Renal insufficiency qualifies as a myeloma-defining CRAB feature when creatinine clearance is <40 mL/min or serum creatinine is >2 mg/dL.
Anemia qualifies as a myeloma-defining CRAB feature when hemoglobin is >2 g/dL below the lower limit of normal or <10 g/dL.
One or more osteolytic lesions on skeletal radiography, CT, or PET-CT qualifies as a myeloma-defining bone lesion.
Clonal bone marrow plasma cells ≥60% is a biomarker myeloma-defining event.
An involved-to-uninvolved serum free light-chain ratio ≥100 is a biomarker myeloma-defining event when the involved free light chain is ≥100 mg/L.
More than one focal lesion on MRI, each at least 5 mm, is a biomarker myeloma-defining event.
Plasma cell leukemia is defined in the review as multiple myeloma with at least 5% circulating plasma cells on a conventional peripheral blood smear.
When multiple myeloma is suspected, the review recommends SPEP, serum immunofixation, and a serum free light-chain assay to evaluate for monoclonal protein.
Mass spectrometry is presented as a more sensitive and specific alternative to SPEP plus serum immunofixation when available.
Bone disease is best assessed with low-dose whole-body CT or PET/CT; MRI is useful for suspected smoldering disease, extramedullary disease, cord compression, or focused symptomatic evaluation.
Conventional skeletal survey is less sensitive than low-dose whole-body CT or PET/CT and is recommended only when advanced imaging is unavailable.
Initial bone marrow evaluation should include FISH or sequencing capable of detecting t(11;14), t(4;14), t(14;16), t(6;14), t(14;20), trisomies, del(17p), del(1p), and gain(1q).
M protein is considered measurable at ≥1 g/dL in serum and/or ≥200 mg/day in urine.
The review recommends monitoring M protein with SPEP and serum free light chains monthly while on therapy and every 3–4 months when off therapy.
Urine protein electrophoresis is recommended at least every 3–6 months to follow urine M protein and detect renal complications with albuminuria.
Approximately 45% of multiple myeloma is hyperdiploid and approximately 40% is IgH-translocated according to the review's molecular classification table.
Among IgH-translocated myeloma, t(11;14) is approximately 20%, t(4;14) 10%, t(6;14) 5%, t(14;16) 4%, and t(14;20) <1% of myeloma cases.
Trisomies and IgH translocations are treated as primary cytogenetic abnormalities, while gain(1q), del(1p), del(17p), and secondary MYC translocations can arise during disease evolution.
High-risk myeloma includes deletion 17p and/or p53 mutation.
High-risk myeloma includes bi-allelic deletion 1p.
High-risk myeloma includes t(4;14), t(14;16), or t(14;20) when accompanied by gain(1q) or del(1p).
High-risk myeloma includes gain(1q) plus del(1p).
mSMART adds plasma cell leukemia, high S phase, extramedullary disease, and double-hit myeloma as high-risk markers beyond the IMS/IMWG cytogenetic definition.
The review reports median survival over 10 years in transplant-eligible myeloma, with 4-year survival estimates above 90%.
In patients older than 65 years, the review reports median survival of approximately 7–8 years and 5-year survival above 70%.
The author notes that current survival estimates likely underestimate outcomes because much of the underlying evidence predates recent immunotherapies.
The author argues that modern risk models have limitations and that individual genomic groups may be more informative than broad heterogeneous risk categories.
Treatment of symptomatic newly diagnosed myeloma is organized primarily by ASCT eligibility, frailty, and risk stratification.
Low-dose dexamethasone at 40 mg once weekly is preferred in most myeloma regimens to reduce toxicity.
For standard-risk ASCT-eligible patients, the author favors Dara-VRd or Isa-VRd for 3–4 cycles followed by early ASCT and maintenance.
For responding standard-risk patients who defer ASCT, stem cells should be collected after the first 3–4 induction cycles and ASCT considered at first relapse.
For high-risk ASCT-eligible patients, the author favors Dara-VRd or Isa-VRd for 3–4 cycles followed by ASCT and maintenance.
For significant pre-existing or treatment-emergent neuropathy, Dara-KRd is presented as an alternative to Dara-VRd or Isa-VRd.

For acute renal failure suspected from light-chain cast nephropathy, the author favors daratumumab plus VCd with plasma exchange or high-cutoff dialysis until free light chains fall and chemotherapy becomes effective.
Once-weekly subcutaneous bortezomib is preferred for most patients receiving initial therapy unless rapid disease control is urgently needed.
For transplant-ineligible patients who are not frail, the author favors Dara-VRd or Isa-VRd for about 6 months followed by maintenance; DRd or VRd are alternatives when quadruplets are inaccessible.
For frail transplant-ineligible patients, the author favors DRd or Isa-Rd for about 6 months followed by maintenance.
In frail older patients, lenalidomide dose should be reduced and dexamethasone can start at 20 mg weekly, be tapered after 4–6 cycles, and be discontinued after the first year when feasible.
ASCT should be considered in eligible patients; in standard-risk patients responding well, it may be performed early or delayed until first relapse if stem cells are harvested early.
Tandem ASCT and routine post-ASCT consolidation are not recommended outside clinical trials.
Lenalidomide plus daratumumab or isatuximab is the author's standard maintenance approach for most patients after initial therapy.
Maintenance begins after ASCT for transplanted patients and after about 6 months of initial therapy for transplant-ineligible patients or those deferring transplant.
Lenalidomide maintenance is given for 2 years in standard-risk myeloma and until progression or unacceptable toxicity in high-risk myeloma; anti-CD38 maintenance is continued until progression.
In standard-risk patients who underwent ASCT and have been MRD-negative for at least 1 year, anti-CD38 maintenance can be stopped after 2 years.
Bortezomib plus lenalidomide is an alternative maintenance option for high-risk myeloma.
Lenalidomide maintenance is associated in the review with a 2- to 3-fold increase in second cancers and requires counseling and monitoring.
The author notes concern for greater cardiac toxicity with carfilzomib and cites ENDURANCE as showing no benefit of KRd over VRd in standard-risk newly diagnosed myeloma.
In S0777, median progression-free survival was 31 months with Rd and 43 months with VRd (p=0.002).

canonical_statement: At relapse, regimen selection should account for timing of relapse, response to prior therapy, aggressiveness, and performance status (TRAP).
When a triplet regimen is used at relapse, the author recommends including at least two drugs to which the patient is not refractory.
For lenalidomide-refractory relapse, pomalidomide-based regimens are preferred over lenalidomide-containing regimens.
Patients eligible for ASCT should be considered for salvage transplant if they never had one, or after a prior ASCT when the first remission lasted at least 36 months with maintenance.
Daratumumab-based triplets are major first-relapse options when the patient is not refractory to daratumumab.
Teclistamab plus daratumumab is presented as a major first- or second-relapse option for patients not refractory to daratumumab.
Patients receiving teclistamab plus daratumumab should receive routine monthly IVIG regardless of immunoglobulin level because of the high infection risk.
BCMA-targeting bispecific antibodies are major options in relapsed myeloma; prophylactic tocilizumab can reduce cytokine release syndrome and monthly IVIG is recommended because of infection risk.
Major adverse effects of bispecific antibodies include cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, infections, and cytopenias.

quantitative_result.original_result_text: CRS, neurotoxicity, infections, and cytopenias were identified as major adverse effects.

canonical_statement: Talquetamab is best reserved for later-line therapy or short-term bridging to CAR-T because of dysgeusia, appetite loss, nail changes, skin toxicity, and weight loss.

CAR-T therapy is a major option in first or second relapse and offers a one-time treatment with the possibility of prolonged treatment-free remission, but requires lead time and adequate disease control.

The review identifies cytokine release syndrome, neurotoxicity, prolonged cytopenias, infection, immune effector cell enterocolitis, and rare Parkinson-like features after cilta-cel as CAR-T safety concerns.
Belantamab mafodotin is associated with keratopathy in approximately 70%–80% of patients, with grade 3–4 keratopathy in about 30% under usual dosing.
After an initial response to belantamab mafodotin, reducing frequency to one dose every 2–3 months may reduce keratopathy severity and treatment disruption.
Carfilzomib has lower neurotoxicity than bortezomib but serious cardiac adverse effects occur in a small proportion of patients, reported as about 5%.

Venetoclax is considered investigational in myeloma and should be restricted to relapsed t(11;14) disease with limited options because a randomized trial showed excess mortality despite deeper responses and better PFS.
At first relapse, the author prefers cilta-cel or Tec-Dara for anti-CD38-sensitive disease, and cilta-cel or a BCMA-directed bispecific for anti-CD38-refractory disease.
At second or later relapse, the author prioritizes CAR-T, bispecifics, belantamab combinations, or standard triplets, sequencing options according to prior therapy and target exposure.
For disease refractory to IMiDs, proteasome inhibitors, anti-CD38 antibodies, and BCMA-directed approaches, options include talquetamab, venetoclax for t(11;14), or alkylator-based regimens.
If relapse occurs more than 24–36 months after stopping therapy, the initial successful regimen can be re-used when feasible.
For some relapsed regimens, especially bispecific antibodies and proteasome inhibitors, the author considers stopping therapy after an excellent response to reduce serious toxicity.
In KarMMa-3, median progression-free survival was 4.4 months with a standard regimen and 13.3 months with ide-cel (p<0.001).

canonical_statement: Zoledronic acid or pamidronate is recommended for all myeloma patients, and dosing every 3–4 months may provide similar protection with fewer adverse effects than monthly dosing.

Denosumab is an alternative bone-modifying agent, especially with significant renal dysfunction; after denosumab discontinuation, a bisphosphonate dose should be considered to reduce rebound osteoclast activity.
Prophylactic levofloxacin for the first 2–3 months of initial therapy should be considered to reduce serious infection risk.
Long-term Pneumocystis prophylaxis with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or an alternative should be considered for patients receiving long-term steroids or anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody therapy.
Acyclovir or valacyclovir should be routinely administered for patients receiving proteasome inhibitors, anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies, or elotuzumab to prevent herpes zoster.
IVIG should be given routinely to patients receiving bispecific antibodies and considered in hypogammaglobulinemic patients receiving daratumumab.
The review notes inadequate COVID vaccine responses in myeloma and recommends booster vaccination as advised.
Within the current SMM definition, the review distinguishes high-risk disease with about 25% annual progression risk in the first 2 years from low-risk disease with about 5% annual progression risk.
Mayo 2018 high-risk SMM criteria are serum M protein >2 g/dL, involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio >20, and bone marrow plasma cells >20%; any 2–3 factors define high-risk SMM.

Additional high-risk SMM features include evolving M protein, 50%–60% clonal marrow plasma cells, t(4;14), del(17p), gain(1q), increased circulating plasma cells, diffuse or single-focal-lesion MRI abnormalities, and PET-CT focal uptake without osteolysis.
Presence of 2 or 3 Mayo 2018 risk factors is associated with a median time to progression to multiple myeloma of approximately 2 years.
The author recommends daratumumab for newly diagnosed high-risk SMM and observation without therapy for other SMM patients.
If SMM shows evolving monoclonal protein or transitions from low/intermediate to high risk, daratumumab should be considered.
In AQUILA, 5-year progression-free survival (time to active myeloma) was 40.8% with active monitoring and 63.1% with 3 years of daratumumab; the review reports a 51% risk reduction (p<0.001).

population.label: High-risk smoldering multiple myeloma in AQUILA

quantitative_result.original_result_text: In AQUILA, 5-year progression-free survival (time to active myeloma) was 40.8% with active monitoring and 63.1% with 3 years of daratumumab; the review reports a 51% risk reduction (p<0.001).

canonical_statement: In AQUILA, 5-year overall survival was 93.0% with daratumumab and 86.9% with active monitoring (HR 0.52, 95% CI 0.27–0.98).

quantitative_result.original_result_text: Overall survival at 5 years was 93.0% with daratumumab and 86.9% with active monitoring; hazard ratio 0.52 (95% CI 0.27–0.98).
